rationale: A wins because it knows where the floor ends: it turns weak facts into proof asks instead of decorating them into claims. A's "Linear is expanding into a new market without the SaaS growth playbook" works because it immediately demands "on-record confirmation" of the no-sales premise; B's "It's Not Building a Sales Team to Do It" states the unproven thing as the headline. B then adds "Productboard, Aha!, and Jira" and "tools that have long drawn complaints" — sharper copy, shakier sourcing. That's how angles get a founder excited and a reporter annoyed.
gaps_in_A: "taking on the product-management stack" is a little ahead of the supplied facts. Roadmapping and stakeholder views imply adjacency, but not full-stack displacement without feature depth, pricing, or named switchers.

"The prevailing belief: expanding beyond your core persona requires a sales-led motion" is plausible, but still an asserted market premise. It needs one or two comparison companies or softer wording before it becomes load-bearing.
The set has the right proof asks, but the accepted angles still depend heavily on unavailable proof: pricing, named beta users, and a real customer count.
gaps_in_B: "It's Not Building a Sales Team to Do It" overclaims. The update says no enterprise sales team is mentioned; it does not say Linear is not building one.
"every software company that successfully expands its addressable market deploys sales headcount and a demand-gen machine" is sweeping, unsupported, and begging to be disproved.
"Productboard, Aha!, and Jira" plus "tools that have long drawn complaints about bloat, slowness, and over-complexity" are imported facts. Maybe true, maybe useful, but not in the update.
"doesn't live in the Terminal" is cute and wrong-adjacent. Keyboard-driven interface does not mean terminal, and "community forums within days" is a fake news peg.
